                                       WATER DATA
                          General Information on Water
   Specific gravity of water is usually given as 1.0 at 60°F. However, for
   some purposes it is given as 1.0 at 39.2°F; the point of maximum
   density. Based on water at 39.2°F as 1.0, water at 60°F has a specific
   gravity of .999. Therefore it makes no practical difference which base
   is selected.

1 Second-Foot (cu.ft. per sec.) of Water = 448.83 GPM
Barrels per day (42 gal) x .02917 = gal. per min.
Pressure, Lb. per Sq. In. to Feet (head) of Water
                             ft. = 2.31 x lb./sq. in.
Pressure, Feet (head) of Water to Lb. per Sq. In.
                            lb./sq. in. = .4331 x ft.
Inches of Mercury (at 32°F) to Feet of Water (at 39.2°F)
                           ft. = 1.133 x in. hg.

   Among the many empirical formulas for friction losses that have
   been proposed, that of Hazen and Williams has been most widely
   used. It states that:
   f = 0.2083

This formula gives accurate values only when the kinematic
   viscosity of the liquids is about 1.1 centistokes or 31.5 SSU, which
   is the case with water at about 60°F. But the viscosity of water
   varies with the temperature, from 1.8 at 32°F, to .29 centistokes at
   212°F. The tables are therefore subject to this error, which may
   increase the friction loss as much as 20% at 32°F and decrease it
   as much as 20% at 212°F. Note that the tables may be used for
   any liquid having a viscosity of the same order as indicated above.
   Values of C for various types of pipe are given below with the

              Friction Losses Through Miscellaneous Fittings
The friction losses below are given for use in making approximate
   estimates of friction loss through fittings not covered elsewhere in
   this book.
They are based on the formula:
v2
    h = k 2g = .0155(k) (v2)
in which; h = head loss due to fitting in feet (this is loss in addition
   to that in a straight pipe the length of the fitting).
k = constant for the type of fitting
   v = velocity in the pipe in feet per second
   g = acceleration due to gravity = about 32.2 feet per second
Type of fitting                       k*

Square elbow (intersection of 2 cylinders at 90°)             1.25
   Square return elbow (180°)                                     2.5
   Angle elbow (intersection of 2 cylinders at an angle
     other than 90°                                        1.25 (angle/90°)2
   Disk or wobble-disk meter                                   3.4 to 10
   Rotary meter (star or cog-wheel piston)                         10
   Reciprocating piston meter                                      15
   Turbine wheel (double-flow, balanced) meter                  5 to 7.5
   Horizontal (lift) check valve                                8 to 12
   Ball check valve                                            65 to 70
Elbows or bends made up of short sections of straight pipe welded
   together or circular bends with corrugated inner radius will have a
   friction loss from 1.3 to 1.6 times greater than that of an equivalent
   smooth elbow or bend.
* Values of k based on those in Hydraulics by Schoder and Dawson
   and the Standards of the Hydraulic Institute.
